title: Developmental milestones, sequence and red flags
blurb: Place key milestones in order across the four domains, correct for prematurity and spot the findings that need referral.
question: A mother says her 2-year-old used to say about 15 words and wave goodbye, but over the last two months has stopped talking and no longer responds to his name. What is the significance of this, and what should the nurse do?

teach.h: Sequence matters more than the exact week
teach.body: Development is assessed across domains: gross motor, fine motor and vision, speech and language, and social and emotional. Children vary in the age they reach each skill, but the ORDER is predictable: head control comes before sitting, sitting before standing, standing before walking. Plain English: judge whether a child is moving forward in the expected sequence, and act on anything that goes backwards.
teach.cite: CDC 'Learn the Signs. Act Early.' milestones, 2022 revision

teach.h: Gross motor sequence (CDC ages most children reach)

items.label: Holds head up when on tummy
Rolls tummy to back; leans on hands to sit
Pulls to stand; cruises along furniture

teach.caption: CDC ages are when about 75% of children show the skill; UK tables may differ slightly. Learn the order.

head: Age
Fine motor / cognitive
Language
Social
rows: Rakes food; passes hand to hand

teach.body: For a baby born preterm, developmental age is calculated from the original due date, not the birth date, until the child is 2 years old. Example: a baby born 10 weeks early who is 7 months old is assessed against roughly a 4.5-month-old's skills.
teach.cite: NHS: your baby's health and development reviews

teach.h: What to do with a concern
teach.caption: NICE CG128: refer children under 3 to the autism team if there is regression in language or social skills. NICE NG62: refer a child not sitting by 8 months or not walking by 18 months (corrected age) to a child development service.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Leo at his 2-year review
items: Leo, 2 years 2 months, is seen by health visitor Amina. His ASQ-3 shows low communication scores.
His father reports Leo had about 15 words at 18 months but has stopped using them and no longer waves or responds to his name.
Amina recognises regression: loss of previously acquired skills is a red flag at any age.
She does not 'wait and see'. She refers promptly (including to the autism team, per NICE CG128), records the history and supports the family.

teach.text: Do not label a child 'delayed' using the birth date if they were born preterm: correct until 2 years. And do not reassure about LOSS of skills: regression is a red flag whatever the child's age.

items: Assess four domains; the sequence is predictable even when timing varies.
Sits unsupported around 9 months, cruises around 1 year, walks alone by about 18 months (CDC).
Pincer grip around 1 year; 3+ words by 18 months; two-word phrases by 2 years (CDC).
Not sitting by 8 months or not walking by 18 months (corrected) = refer to a child development service (NICE NG62).
Loss of previously acquired skills at any age needs prompt referral.

summary: You can now order the main milestones across the four domains, correct a preterm baby's age, and recognise regression as a red flag needing prompt referral. You can also use milestone knowledge to plan age-appropriate care and reassure parents accurately.

A.q: A student nurse asks which sequence of gross motor development is typical in the first 18 months. Which is correct?
options: Sits unsupported, head control, cruises, walks
Head control, sits unsupported, cruises, walks
Head control, cruises, sits unsupported, walks
Sits unsupported, cruises, head control, walks
A.why: Head control comes first (around 2 months on tummy), then sitting without support (about 9 months), cruising (about 1 year) and walking alone (about 18 months).

whyNot.0: Sitting depends on head and trunk control, so head control comes first.
whyNot.2: Cruising needs the trunk control gained when sitting, so sitting comes before cruising.
whyNot.3: Head control is the earliest of these skills, not the third.

A.q: Ayla was born at 32 weeks' gestation and is now 9 months old by her date of birth. Her parents are worried she is not yet sitting without support. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: Assess against a 9-month-old as she is over 6 months
Correction applies to weight, not development
Refer urgently as sitting is overdue at 9 months
Assess against her corrected age of about 7 months
A.why: Developmental age is corrected for prematurity until age 2. Born 8 weeks early, Ayla's corrected age is about 7 months, when not yet sitting unsupported is within the expected range.

whyNot.0: Correction continues until age 2, not 6 months.
whyNot.1: Developmental age is corrected for prematurity as well as growth.
whyNot.2: At her corrected age this is not overdue, so urgent referral is not indicated on this finding.

A.q: Which finding is a developmental red flag at any age?
options: Loss of skills the child already had
Bottom shuffling instead of crawling
Preferring familiar adults to strangers
Babbling before saying real words
A.why: Regression (loss of previously acquired skills) is a red flag at any age and needs prompt referral.

whyNot.1: Some children bottom shuffle rather than crawl; on its own this is a variation of normal.
whyNot.2: Wariness of strangers is an expected social milestone around 9 months.
whyNot.3: Babbling normally comes before first words.

B.q: At a 1-year review, which fine motor skill would the nurse expect most children to show?
options: Building a tower of six bricks
Drawing a person with three body parts
Picking up small food with thumb and finger
Holding a pencil between fingers and thumb
B.why: A pincer grip (thumb and pointer finger) is a 1-year milestone in the CDC list.

whyNot.0: Building taller towers is a later toddler skill.
whyNot.1: Drawing a person with three or more parts is a 4-year milestone.
whyNot.3: Holding a pencil between fingers and thumb rather than in a fist is a 4-year milestone.

B.q: Mason, 18 months, walks alone, scribbles and points to show his father things he finds interesting. He says 'mama', 'dada', 'ball', 'dog' and 'more'. What should the nurse conclude?
options: His development is in line with 18-month milestones
His speech is delayed as he does not join two words
He needs referral as he is not yet running
His pointing suggests a social communication concern
B.why: Walking alone, scribbling, pointing to show interest and 3 or more words besides mama and dada are all 18-month milestones.

whyNot.1: Joining two words is expected by 2 years, not 18 months.
whyNot.3: Pointing to show interest is a positive social communication sign.

B.q: Zara, 9 months, is staying on a surgical ward. Her parents ask the nurse which play will suit her stage. Which activity best fits a typical 9-month-old?
options: A simple jigsaw with 12 pieces
A pretend tea party with a doll
Drawing a picture of her family
Finding a toy hidden under a cloth
B.why: Looking for dropped or hidden objects is a 9-month cognitive milestone, so peek-a-boo and hide-the-toy games suit her stage.

whyNot.0: Jigsaws need fine motor and problem-solving skills well beyond 9 months.
whyNot.1: Pretend play develops in later toddler and preschool years.
whyNot.2: Drawing recognisable figures is a preschool skill.

C.q: Noah, 2 years 3 months, attends for his review. His mother says he had about 20 words and waved goodbye at 18 months but has lost these over the past 3 months and no longer looks up when called. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her that speech often plateaus at this age
Refer him promptly for specialist assessment
Repeat the ASQ-3 in 6 months to check progress
Advise speech games at home and review at 3 years
C.why: Loss of previously acquired language and social skills is regression, a red flag at any age; NICE CG128 advises referral to the autism team for under 3s with regression in language or social skills.

whyNot.0: Reassurance is inappropriate when skills have been lost.
whyNot.2: Delaying assessment for 6 months risks missing a serious condition.
whyNot.3: Home activities may help but do not replace prompt referral for regression.

C.q: A health visitor sees Eva, 10 months, born at term. Eva cannot sit without support, has no babble and does not transfer toys between hands. What is the best interpretation?
options: She is within the normal range for a 10-month-old
Her delay is limited to gross motor skills
She has delay across several domains needing review
She should be assessed at her corrected age
C.why: Sitting unsupported, babbling and transferring are all 9-month milestones, so Eva shows delay across gross motor, language and fine motor domains and needs further assessment.

whyNot.0: Most children sit, babble and transfer objects by 9 months.
whyNot.1: Language and fine motor skills are also delayed.
whyNot.3: Eva was born at term, so no correction applies.

C.q: Which statement about developmental milestones should a nurse share with a worried parent?
options: Children vary in timing, but the order is predictable
Each skill appears in the same week for all children
Prematurity is corrected for until the child is 5
A child who misses one milestone needs urgent referral
C.why: Timing varies between children, but the sequence is predictable; concerns are judged on progress, the pattern of skills and any regression.

whyNot.1: Milestone ages vary; CDC ages reflect when most (about 75%) children show a skill.
whyNot.2: Correction for prematurity applies until 2 years.
whyNot.3: An isolated, slightly late milestone usually needs review rather than urgent referral.

reteach.title: Build the child from the top down
reteach.question: Why does a baby hold up her head months before she can sit, stand or walk?

blocks.body: Motor control spreads downwards: first the head, then the trunk for sitting, then hips and legs for standing and walking. Fine motor control moves from a whole-hand rake (about 9 months) to a neat pincer grip (about 1 year). Language moves from sounds to babble to words to phrases.

blocks.h: Motor skills build on each other

blocks.text: Going forward slowly = review, unless a motor red flag is reached (not sitting by 8 months or not walking by 18 months, corrected: refer, NICE NG62). Going BACKWARDS (losing skills) = refer promptly.

explain.body: Head up on tummy (2 months), rolls tummy to back (6 months), sits unsupported (9 months), pulls to stand and cruises (1 year), walks alone (18 months), runs and kicks a ball (2 years), using CDC ages.

test.q: By which age do most children walk alone (CDC)?
options: 9 months
12 months
2 years
18 months
test.why: Walking alone is listed as an 18-month milestone.

whyNot.0: At 9 months most children are sitting without support.
whyNot.1: At 1 year most children pull to stand and cruise.
whyNot.2: By 2 years children are running and kicking a ball.

explain.body: Rakes and transfers objects (9 months), pincer grip (1 year), scribbles (18 months). Babbles (9 months), mama or dada (1 year), 3 or more words (18 months), two words together (2 years), sentences of 4 or more words (4 years).

test.q: At what age do most children join two words together, such as 'more milk'?
options: 12 months
2 years
18 months
4 years
test.why: Saying at least two words together is a 2-year milestone.

whyNot.0: At 1 year children say single words such as mama or dada.
whyNot.2: At 18 months children use 3 or more single words.
whyNot.3: At 4 years children speak in sentences of 4 or more words.

explain.body: Subtract the weeks born early from the actual age. Use corrected age to judge development until the child is 2 years old.

test.q: Theo was born at 28 weeks and is 8 months old. What is his approximate corrected age for developmental review?
options: 8 months
6 months
5 months
4 months
test.why: Born 12 weeks (about 3 months) early, his corrected age is about 5 months.

whyNot.0: 8 months is his actual age; correction applies until 2 years.
whyNot.1: 6 months would correct by only 2 months.

explain.body: Loss of previously acquired skills at any age needs prompt referral. NICE CG128 advises referring children under 3 to the autism team if language or social skills regress.

test.q: Which history most needs prompt referral?
options: A 2-year-old who has stopped using words he had
A 14-month-old who cruises but does not walk
A 10-month-old who rakes food but has no pincer grip
A 9-month-old who is shy with strangers
test.why: Loss of previously acquired words is regression, a red flag at any age.

whyNot.1: Cruising at 14 months is consistent with normal progression towards walking.
whyNot.2: The pincer grip is expected around 1 year, so raking at 10 months is normal.
whyNot.3: Stranger wariness is an expected 9-month social milestone.
